processing: Black tea in the gongfu manner: withered, rolled, fully oxidised and dried. Little is documented about any special local steps.
harvest_season: Not well documented; as with other Chinese gongfu blacks, spring leaf is usually preferred.
appearance_dry: Typically tight, slim, dark strands, as with other gongfu black teas.
appearance_liquor: Typically a clear red, as with other gongfu black teas.
taste_profile: Few tasting records exist. Gongfu black teas of this kind are typically sweet and mellow.

brewing.notes: Ordinary gongfu black settings; nothing specific to this tea is recorded.

vintage_note: As usual for gongfu black teas, it is sold as current or recent harvest tea, with no established ageing market on record. Ask for the picking year and producer, since the name leans heavily on history.
description:
He Hong, short for Hekou red tea, takes its name from Hekou, the old river trading town in Yanshan county in northeast Jiangxi. Hekou was once counted among the four great towns of Jiangxi, and the tea is tied up with its trading past.

The method is little documented. It is a black tea, and as with other gongfu blacks you can assume the usual route of withering, rolling, oxidising and drying, without any recorded local twist.

Expect what is typical of the class: tight dark leaf, a clear red cup and a sweet, mellow flavour. Brew it as you would any good gongfu black, with short steeps first, and form your own view.

Today it is a small, locally promoted name, and old trade stories are part of the pitch. Buy on smell and taste, and ask who made it and where in Yanshan, rather than relying on its historic reputation.
history:
Hekou was a major trading town on the Ming and Qing river routes, promoted today as a leading stop on the Tea Road to Russia: travel writing describes tea from around Wuyi moving through its docks north via Jiujiang and Wuchang to Zhangjiakou, or south towards Guangzhou.

A Ming origin for He Hong and its title as the first Chinese black tea are repeated in local and travel writing, but firm historical evidence is thin, and both should be read as local tradition.
